title: Sheltering in the mountains
intro: A shelter should match the forecast, terrain, group, trip length and ability to retreat. No tent, cave or hut makes an exposed location safe in every storm; check local rules and conditions, and leave a plan with someone responsible.
heroAlt: A tent city at the Kahiltna Glacier base camp

sections.heading: Mountain tents
sections.text: Four-season tents are designed for wind, cold and snow loading better than lightweight summer models, but performance depends on design, condition, site and correct pitching. Select a protected, legal campsite away from avalanche paths, cornices, rockfall and water channels.

details.label: When used
details.text: Overnight camps on treks, alpine routes and expeditions when a portable enclosed shelter is appropriate.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Reusable, relatively quick to establish, and protection from wind, precipitation and insects.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Adds weight; can fail in extreme wind or snow, and still needs a safe site and ventilation.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Choose protected ground outside hazard runouts, orient for expected wind, secure every anchor and manage condensation.

sections.alt: Expedition tents pitched together on a glacier at Kahiltna base camp

sections.heading: Bivouacs and bivy sacks
sections.text: A planned bivouac is a minimal overnight stop; a bivy sack adds weather protection around a sleeping bag, while a bivy shelter offers more structure. Both suit climbers prioritizing low weight or facing an unplanned delay, but offer limited room and can expose users to condensation, wind and cold.

details.label: When used
details.text: Short alpine routes, planned lightweight overnights or emergency delays when retreat is not immediately possible.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Low weight and small packed size; a bivy can be used where pitching a tent is impractical.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Limited comfort and weather protection; moisture management and site selection are critical.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Choose the safest available sheltered site, insulate from the ground and protect breathing space from snow.

sections.alt: A climber's hanging bivouac camp on El Capitan

sections.heading: Snow caves, igloos and trenches
sections.text: Snow shelters can provide insulation when suitable snow is available and builders have trained for the task. Snow conditions and terrain vary, and excavation can cause collapse, burial or suffocation. A snow shelter is not an improvised substitute for a tent without training and careful ventilation.

details.label: When used
details.text: In suitable snow conditions, typically by people with practice and an appropriate reason to build one.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Snow can insulate from wind and cold; a built shelter may be quieter and more stable than an exposed bivouac.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Construction takes time and energy; collapse, ventilation failure and hazardous snowpack are serious risks.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Use a site outside avalanche terrain and follow trained shelter-building practice; maintain ventilation and monitor conditions.

sections.alt: A snow cave entrance dug into a snowbank on Mount Hood

sections.heading: Mountain huts and refuges
sections.text: Huts range from staffed refuges to basic emergency shelters. Reservations, access rules, services and seasonal opening vary, so check directly with the hut operator. A refuge is not a guarantee of space or rescue, and busy huts can require carrying backup food and shelter.

details.label: When used
details.text: Established routes with a hut network, especially where weather or terrain makes a fixed shelter useful.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Reduces carried shelter weight and may provide beds, meals, water or local route information.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Can be full, closed or inaccessible; comfort and services vary and require advance planning.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Confirm booking and opening status, follow hut rules, and retain a contingency plan for a missed arrival.

sections.alt: The Glecksteinhütte mountain refuge in the Swiss Alps

sections.heading: Base camps
sections.text: A base camp is a relatively established staging area used for acclimatization, rest, communication and expedition logistics. It should be located with attention to avalanches, rockfall, flooding, sanitation, waste and the needs of nearby communities.

details.label: When used
details.text: Longer remote expeditions where a stable operations point supports multiple trips to higher terrain.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Offers a place to rest, organize supplies and coordinate with the team over an extended trip.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Can become crowded and environmentally damaging; remoteness complicates supply and evacuation.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Use established sites and local guidance; plan waste, water, communications and emergency procedures before arrival.

sections.alt: A large expedition base camp at Kahiltna Glacier

sections.heading: High camps
sections.text: High camps are temporary staging points above base camp, used to support acclimatization or an ascent. Exposure, altitude and weather make them more demanding; camp placement and any fixed equipment must be planned by experienced teams for the specific route.

details.label: When used
details.text: On high-altitude objectives where the itinerary and route conditions call for intermediate camps.

details.label: Advantages
details.text: Can break a long ascent into stages and provide a planned place to rest or wait for conditions.

details.label: Disadvantages
details.text: Cold, wind, altitude illness and objective hazards intensify; camps may be exposed or difficult to evacuate.

details.label: Basic setup
details.text: Follow an expedition plan, monitor health and weather, secure shelter and be prepared to descend rather than push on.

sections.alt: A small tent camp high on Mount Everest
